utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it please the Court, may I address the Court for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We raised an issue last night at the end of the hearing in regards to the amount of time for cross-examination as direct examination. I have, if the usher would help me, a copy of a ruling this Trial Chamber made on the 10th day of June, for the record, page 12248, lines 13 through 23. Give them to everybody. Thank you. While the usher is passing those out, Your Honour, that was the witness Mr. Pasalic. In that ruling, Your Honour, Mr. President, as you can well see, starting at line 13 and ending at line 23, starting line 14, the second sentence, "But as a principle in this trial, we will give equal time to the direct examination as to the cross-examination." That is the most recent ruling, and we believe that is the ruling of this Trial Chamber. I understand Your Honours were going to make a decision this morning -- perhaps you've already made your decision -- but I wanted to have you bear that in mind. We would like to have rules that we can abide by and that don't change daily or weekly. Number 2, for the future -- this issue is passed now with this witness. In regards to the issue brought up yesterday concerning his accidental wounding or killing of a man in a restaurant, and in answer to Judge Clark's question, when Falk Simang was on the stand, the issue we were raising was the fact that Falk Simang not only killed people but he robbed them. Robbery is a crime involving truth and veracity whereas accidental killing is not. This issue may come back up in future witnesses, and I'm just asking the Court to take notice of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, thank you very much to draw our attention to the ruling made by this Trial Chamber on this very issue. Yes, Mr. Stringer, I apologise for not allowing you to take the floor yesterday afternoon because of the time limit. Now, this Trial Chamber would like to hear the views from the Prosecution on this very issue. You may have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. On the broader issue of time to be allowed for cross-examination, Mr. Scott is going to address the Trial Chamber on that. I'm going to limit myself simply to responding to the last point raised by counsel, that is the cross-examination as to the incident in the restaurant. As the Trial Chamber will recall, after establishing with the witness that the event in fact took place, I went directly to what is the relevant -- the relevance of the question, which was the extent to which he was assisted or the extent to which Mr. Naletilic intervened on his behalf, which, in our view, would have raised an issue as to his credibility, frankly speaking, his willingness to come, appear before the Trial Chamber and lie about Mr. Naletilic's position within the Convicts Battalion based on any intervention that Mr. Naletilic may have made on his behalf in respect of that incident. So it does go to credibility. And if there wasn't a tie-in along those lines, I doubt that I would have raised the issue at all. And I believe, Mr. President, Mr. Scott can raise -- or address you on the other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've raised this matter with the Chamber before, respectfully, to you and Judge Diarra and Judge Clark. We are increasingly concerned on behalf of the Prosecution with finishing this part of the Defence case. We are also very concerned, frankly, about the application of any artificial limits -- what we would consider, respectfully, artificial limits on an effective cross-examination. Let's be transparent: It is very easy for these Defence witnesses, who have access, Your Honour, to a whole category of witnesses and persons who, frankly, the OTP does not have access to. They can trot HVO insiders through here day after day, saying all sorts of things. And it will be our position, it is our position - and again I'm going to be perfectly transparent - partisan witnesses who will come in here and we believe say all numbers of things to defend Mr. Naletilic based on past loyalty, past close association, based on common political views, based on current associations and events going on outside The Hague; all those matters require time to fully ventilate. It is one thing for the -- excuse me, I'm on -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you have to be very polite until Mr. Scott finishes his argument. He is addressing the Court, not you. You have to understand that. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sure Mr. Krsnik will object strongly to my comments, and I expect him to, but I'm going to make this very clear to the Chamber this morning and will continue to in the days ahead, as necessary. It is very easy to bring a witness in here, ask a few questions, whether it's a 20 minute direct -- "Was Mr. Naletilic ever the commander of the KB?" That takes about 30 seconds to ask. "Did you ever see him on a battlefield?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That takes about 30 seconds to ask. "Did you ever hear him make an anti-Muslim statement?" That takes about 30 seconds to ask. The Defence ask those questions, they sit down, and I suppose -- is the cross-examination then going to be limited to three minutes? It takes more time, Your Honours, especially with hostile witnesses who we've never deposed, we have never seen this witnesses until they walk into this courtroom, we have no prior statements because we have been provided no disclosure in this case, none. It takes time. And let me respectfully submit to the Chamber it is in your interest - I mean that with all respect - it is your interest that this evidence is fully ventilated. You will have the difficult, as you well know, responsibility of writing a judgement in this case. Respectfully, Your Honours, you will not be assisted in doing so if this evidence is not and these witnesses are not fully ventilated. I am very concerned. I think we are entering a dangerous phase in this case in a number of respects, and the Prosecution, as we've said before -- I may not get on my feet and raise my voice the way Mr. Krsnik does and then repeatedly have to apologise to this Chamber for my conduct, but I can assure the Chamber the Prosecution feels just as strongly about these matters and just as strongly about receiving a fair trial, and that the Prosecutor receive a fair trial, the international community that we represent receives a fair trial, and that the victims of these alleged crimes receive a fair trial. In order to receive a fair trial and to assist this Chamber in reaching a proper judgement - good or bad for the Prosecution but a proper judgement - this evidence must be fully ventilated and I ask the Chamber not to impose -- not to be quick to impose artificial limits on effective cross-examination. I also want to mention to the Chamber a couple of other points. Your Honour, I know it's taking time but we view these as highly important matters, highly important. In terms of the cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses, we did a very quick search of just the first few weeks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There were at least nine witnesses, off the top, the cross-examination, was longer than the direct examination. In terms of the Defence -- I'm going to tie this in now, Your Honour, to the Defence request for breaks before and after the depositions. The long and short of the two motions is they want a break before the depositions and another break after the depositions. To some degree -- I want to be very careful in what I say. To some degree we would not oppose that, all other things being equal, but there is the rub. We do not agree to any breaks and we will oppose any breaks to the extent that it prejudices the Prosecution's ability to deal with this case. Now, it's up to the Defence to call their witnesses and put on their case. That's their prerogative. We understand that. But frankly, Your Honour, it's our position, respectfully, if the Defence wants to take ten weeks to call about 18 witnesses, many long background witnesses, many repetitive witnesses on the referendum in 1992, and they find themselves caught short on time at the end, that's their judgement, that's the decisions that they made. But I object, and on the behalf of the Prosecution team, Mr. Stringer, myself, Mr. Bos, Mr. Poriouvaev, object to the Prosecution case being prejudiced by rushing at the end of this to finish the Defence case because of the time considerations that they have raised. They call all the witnesses, these long witnesses who went on for days that they wanted to call. And we will object to any breaks in the trial schedule which creates a pressure to finish the case which then in turn creates a pressure on the Prosecution not to be able to effectively cross-examine these Defence witnesses. I repeat what I said a few moments ago: I am very concerned that we are approaching a very dangerous phase in this case. Dangerous to fairness to both parties, danger to getting at the truth. And some of the issues that we are going to raise with these next witnesses are going to be important, but they are not susceptible to short treatment. I submit respectfully, if the Chamber does not hear some of this information, you will be poorly served. And you will be making -- ultimately making judgements without having important information available to. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, continuing with the motions filed by the Defence counsel on the matter of the break, Mr. Scott, are you going to submit us with a written response on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you wish, I will, of course, Mr. President, but I can tell you right now the written response -- I'll take the transcript and it will be the comments that I've just made. We are opposed to any breaks before or after the deposition to the extent they create an unfair pressure on the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Mr. Krsnik, you have to be very concise to present your points. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I know I have to be very concise and I know from the beginning, since I first came to this Tribunal, I've been listening about the fairness, about the equal treatment, I've been listening about the international community, as if I were not a member of this international community, as if the international community is not concerned if there are delusions and there are violations, if there is deceit, and as if it is not going to be concerned if the Prosecution is resorting to means which are not fair, which are not allowed. And the Defence has every reason to doubt that that is the case, and it has already witnessed that. It has been saying that before this Chamber for a number of months now. My learned friends, Prosecutors, cannot make any rules about anything; it is only the Chamber that can do that. My learned friend always calls upon one and only thing, and insists on him having more rights than anybody else. That cannot be true. Your Honours, yesterday I showed you a clipping from the newspaper, and it was a striking example -- I didn't want to waste much more time on that, but the question is how come that the Sarajevo media can have an expert testimony a month before the witness actually appears before the Court? How come journalists can come by the names of our witnesses? How and why are newspaper articles printed after every witness, Defence witness, we have here? We have proof, and Mr. Scott recognised it to me when somebody said -- when I asked him whether he spoke to a journalist and he said yes, but he didn't want to give it to me in writing, although he did confirm it verbally to me. Mr. Scott behaves, together with the Prosecution, as if it was impossible to lose a case. It is not about a victory or a defeat. It is about fairness and justice. Mr. Scott wants -- is telling us, "What I say is the truth, what others say is -- raises ground for suspicion." How and with what right does he today comment upon the things that he is going to be able to present in his final letter, brief? How dares he judge the testimonies of the witnesses who have not even appeared before this Court yet? Who gives him this right? Yes, Your Honours, honourable Mr. President, if anybody was to be happy if the rules were equal and served fairness, so if anybody were to be happy if that was true, then it would be me, but I cannot confirm that this fairness, this equal treatment, the equality of rules, exists. I'm going to say this openly, and I have the feeling in this courtroom -- not in this court -- not in this courtroom because I respect the efforts of this Trial Chamber and I appreciate your sense of justice and your sense of trying to be fair to everybody, but walking around this Tribunal, tending to my business, I can say this publicly, that this Tribunal either is, or is perceived by the Prosecution, as belonging to the Prosecution. All the rest of us are not very welcome here. Your Honours, I'm asking you now -- obviously you don't know everything that is happening beyond these walls, behind our backs. My witnesses have come from Herzegovina very, very disturbed and distressed because the investigators are calling them for interviews on the request of this Prosecution, and we said at the beginning that we should not communicate with each other's witnesses. So we from the Defence should not communicate with Prosecution witnesses and vice versa. Why is this being done? To intimidate the witnesses. Because it seems that Mr. Scott cannot face the feeling of maybe facing a defeat in this case. The investigators who invited these witnesses for interviews, my Defence interviews -- and this is a serious matter. Your Honours, I've been suffering that for two years now, and nobody is there to help me. When I say something before this Trial Chamber, the answer is, "Okay," but that is overlooked. The same thing happened when Mr. Scott uttered the name of a protected witness. He apologised but that was all. Okay. I understand that to err is human, but still, it was a big mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you made very serious allegations against the Prosecutor, especially Mr. Scott. If you have some evidence, we would like to have it, but now is not the time for this kind of argument. I understand that on many points, on many areas, there is no agreement between the two parties, but right now we have a witness waiting outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. This is exactly my concern. I have seven witnesses waiting here and I believe that this Honourable Court understands the difference. Background witnesses require more time, and I want to bring this case to an end according to your decision on the beginning of depositions, and we have determined that our witnesses would be background witnesses, both for the indictment as well as for the allegations presented before this courtroom. These are my witnesses, Defence witnesses. I will take 40 times to examine them, and my learned friends from the Prosecution have the right to cross-examine them. I have about 15 more witnesses to examine within the next eight days before the end of depositions. All the witnesses are ready, and if somebody is asking for some new time, for more time, then we would be talking about inconsistency because there have been 20 of your rulings in the past to the effect that the cross-examination can only last as long as the examination-in-chief. And as for my allegations, Your Honours, that I have just proposed, I am going to invite the witness who was told that this was the last opportunity for him to appear before the Tribunal, the witness replied, "I'm going to come to the Tribunal and let the Prosecution examine me there." Many of my witnesses have said that. And you saw the evidence, the article, from the newspaper. Doesn't that call for an investigation? How did that reach the newspapers? Does it not call for an investigation to investigate the relationship between the Defence witnesses and the Prosecution? I am preparing a study about the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina in which I'm going to describe everything in that broad study, as per your request, as per your very justified request, Your Honours. I've already pointed out to an inadmissible relationship of the interested parties and very subjective secret services which are very, very, very interested in the outcome of the cases before this Trial Chamber, and here, nobody dares say whether this is just, whether this is fair. Are they really interested in justice? Aren't they going to be detrimental for the international community? Thank you. That will be all from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric? You have to understand we are under time pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I understand that we are all under time constraints, but this is not the Krsnik case but this is the case against Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Martinovic. Therefore I am allowed to say at least two sentences and I will say them. Our learned friends from the Prosecution are entitled to their position, and nobody has the right to deny them their right to their position. That's what the procedure is for. The procedure is everything. And above the procedure, there is nothing but the sky. That is a very well-known statement by a French philosopher. In order to respect this procedure, we are asked to be consistent, so the consistency has to be abided by the Prosecution as well. A certain while ago, our colleagues complained that they were under pressure because they didn't have the time to prepare for their cross-examination; they did not -- they were not provided with the names of witnesses in time; they do not have the sequence of witnesses. Now, when the Defence is asking for the minimum of tolerance, when they are -- it provides them with the lists of witnesses, when we have problems with the transportation -- the 15th is the last day for the depositions. After that, the first flight out of Mostar is on Wednesday. The Prosecution says that the pressure on time, the burden of that time, is on them, but they have more time than us. They are not consistent. Who has to suffer from the pressure of time most? It is our clients who are in gaol and they have asked their Defence counsels to prepare the defence as best as they can. This is our case, our part of the case, Your Honours. You're going to issue the ruling according to your conscience, according to your profession, and we are never going to object to that ruling. We will not have the break, but I am asking everybody to respect the procedure. I'm asking everybody to consider -- to be consistent. Our learned friend Scott was very subjective and very inconsistent in what he said last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber is seized of this oral motion to shorten the time of cross-examination by the Prosecution of the present witness on the basis of the principle of equality of arms. We made a ruling the other day that both parties will be given more or less the same amount of time in conducting direct and cross-examinations. In principle, we would like to adhere to this ruling. Taking into consideration that principle of equality of arms should not be interpreted literally as an exact amount of time used by each party in every case, the issue here is whether one party is put into more disadvantaged position than the other. We appreciate the efforts made by Defence counsel to speed up the direct examination, which shows the full professionalism. I must say, especially with that expert witness, the Defence case was put clearly in the six points of the conclusion of the expert witness's statement. And Mr. Krsnik did well by drawing our attention to certain points instead of lengthy and repetitive direct examination. This practice should be encouraged. It is not only the right of the accused to have a fair and expeditious trial, it is also the requirement of the interests of justice to move faster. To be fair, and out of the interests of justice, in this situation, the other party will have a little more time for the cross-examination of the expert witness. Since the current witness, as Mr. Krsnik rightly put it, is the first fact witness from the Convicts Battalion, and which is the subject matter of this case, and Mr. Meek efficiently conducted his direct examination in a very effective way which touches upon many important issues, in light of the arguments put forward by both parties in yesterday and today's hearing, and out of the interests of justice, after consultations among the judges, we decided to give more time to the Prosecution to conduct the cross-examination. By doing so, we find no prejudice to both parties since they still have the opportunity to clear up certain focused points in dispute in re-examinations and questions out of Judges' questions. Judging from the previous cross-examination with other witnesses, we have no doubt at all that the Prosecution will conduct the cross-examination efficiently and effectively with a reasonable and limited time period. We have spent about 35 minutes on those procedural issues. I hope this decision is clear. Could we have the witness, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, Your Honour, could we have a little guidance in how much time is going to be allowed? Is it -- they have already used 150 per cent of the time I used on direct. Is there some time limit or do they just go on until Your Honours say stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, maybe you could tell us how much time you are going to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thirty minutes maximum, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think it's a reasonable time, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, we would object to that and we would issue and ask the Court to enter a continuing objection, for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, your objection is registered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Would you please sit down. Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you are ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll ask the witness be shown Exhibit P490, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Stringer: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I believe yesterday you testified that one place in which you did participate in a military operation of the Convicts Battalion was at a place called Djubrani. Do I have that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, generally or approximately, where is this place Djubrani located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above Bijelo Polje, towards Siroki Brijeg, up in the hills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've been shown an exhibit, P490. Underneath the English translation, you'll see the document in your language. This operation at Djubrani, did it take place in early July, 1993? Are you able to recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th of June, 1993, until late November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document in front of you, sir - you can look at the Croatian language version - I'll ask you to look at the second page. You've got it now. The second page of that. Does this appear to be a report issued by Miljenko Lasic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his name is here, Miljenko Lasic, but I never saw any papers because I never had anything to do with papers. I never saw this before. This is the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Lasic was the commander of the southeast Herzegovina operative zone of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, you testified that the Convicts Battalion did not have any Bofors. I want to direct your attention to the first page of this document, please. The Croatian language version, if you have it. The second paragraph under the word "Report" says, "Last night we sent a 14.5 PAM mounted on a vehicle to Djubrani at the request of the commander of the forward command post and 80 pieces of 40 millimetre L60 ammunition for a Bofors gun in Tuta's unit." Now, sir, this document is dated two days after the time you just testified you were in Djubrani. Isn't it true that you were in Djubrani, sir, with a Bofors gun of the Kaznjenicka Bojna?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All we had, a Browning 12.7, I never saw any Bofors up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reference here to Tuta's unit, sir, that's the Kaznjenicka Bojna, isn't it? The Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we didn't have a Bofors; 12.7 Browning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move to the next document, sir, just let me ask you, you testified -- I want to make sure I understand your testimony correctly from yesterday. You said that you were working a 12.7 millimetre Browning gun. When you were doing that, were you working together with Mr. Simang and Mr. Mrachacz? When you were -- I'll ask the question again. The Browning gun, did you operate that gun together with Mr. Simang and Mr. Mrachacz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not a gun. It's an anti-aircraft weapon, Browning 12.7. They were assisting me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they were assisting you, you were communicating with your commanders through the use of a Motorola?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were positioned in the Mostar area, sir, did you target any of the mosques that were in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever ordered to fire on mosques in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever fire on mosques in Mostar with the Bofors gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never had it so how could I fire from it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that on the 9th of May, 1993, you were sent to a place close to Mostar with Simang and Mrachacz; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the hill called Galac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Galac hill, is it possible to see down into the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not all of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were sent there, I take it, with other members of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were only three of us, but below us was the Siroki Brijeg Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So other units from Siroki Brijeg also went to Mostar on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were around on Galac, manning the lines in case the BH Army attempted to break through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of day were you contacted by Mr. Andabak and sent to Galac hill on the 9th of May? What time was it, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time? In the morning, around 8.00, is when he called me and told me to go out to the Galac hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say was happening in Mostar at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't tell me anything. He simply told me we should go to the reserve position in case the line was broken through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were other members of the Convicts Battalion sent also to Mostar that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can recall, we were the only three who went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- have you ever heard of the ATG Baja Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their commander was Predrag Mandic, Lija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were -- they didn't stay in Siroki Brijeg, sir, they stayed in the Heliodrom complex; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Predrag Mandic in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would he meet with in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the ATG Baja Kraljevic associated with the Convicts Battalion in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a different unit. They were at the Heliodrom and we were in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness be shown Exhibit P471, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a place called Boksevica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't recall being involved in any combat operations in Boksevica around the 21st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I can see the top couple of pages is the exhibit. I think you've got two exhibits there. The one underneath, the list, is not the one I'm asking for. Just go down to the dividers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a combat report regarding the location Boksevica. Do you know whether Mladen Naletilic was at that location on the -- on or about the 21st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. What might he be doing at Boksevica? I don't remember. This is the first time I see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness be shown Exhibit P611.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that exhibit is coming, sir, let me ask you whether you ever were present during military operations in a place called Rastani, just north of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not in August of 1993 or September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a moment to look at this document, sir. Do you know who Bruno Stojic is or was at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard about Bruno Stojic on television. I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a high level official of the HVO in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that. This is the first time I lay my eyes on these papers. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to read paragraph number 1 of that document to yourself. Do you know if other members of the Convicts Battalion were involved in combat operations in Rastani in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that as indicated in this document, Tuta was the commander of the Convicts Battalion in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your testimony, sir, that Mr. Andabak was the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Andabak was the commander and Zeljko Vukoja, after Cikota was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your testimony, sir, that Mr. Andabak was the highest ranking member of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he had some health problems; sugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had to take insulin for diabetes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the campaign against the Serbs in 1992, do you recall if he also had a drinking problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that. All I know is that he had problems with sugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown Exhibit P663.1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that's coming sir, let me ask you: Did you ever see Mr. Naletilic in Siroki Brijeg during 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have seen him in Siroki Brijeg in a coffee shop or somewhere, but I do not really remember it because it was nine years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the document that's in front of you relates to six prisoners going to work at the Zeljko Bosnjak ATG base in Ljubuski. My question, couple of questions, sir: Zeljko Bosnjak, do you know who that is? There was a man named Zeljko Bosnjak, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I do not know the gentleman nor did I ever see this paper before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Zeljko Bosnjak, was he killed in operations, combat operations, in Rastani in the late summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking back, sir, at this document, doesn't it appear, sir, that the typewritten part of this document, next to the stamp, indicates that the commander of the Convicts Battalion was Mladen Naletilic, Tuta?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Court, my only objection is that this witness has already testified he's never seen this document, the document speaks for itself, and I think on those grounds, the question is irrelevant, immaterial and incompetent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You said the document speaks for itself. The document says that your client, Mr. Naletilic, is the commander of that Convicts Battalion. Now, in this case, I would like to allow the Prosecutor to continue this question so that your witness will have an opportunity to deny or to agree with the accusations from the Prosecutor. I think it's fair. Mr. Stringer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the handwritten signature on this document, is that the signature of Ivan Andabak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I do not know that. This is the first time that I see this paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if Mr. Andabak had been signing orders on behalf of Mr. Naletilic, you wouldn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw any papers at all, nor anyone ever gave me any papers. I do not know who signed them. This is the first time I see this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness to be shown Exhibit P601.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact is, sir, that as a foot soldier of the Kaznjenicka Bojna, it's quite possible that you would not have known the extent to which Mladen Naletilic exercised control over the Convicts Battalion during 1993; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not so. He could not command it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me, sir, that the documents that we have been reviewing here would indicate otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can say anything it likes. I never saw such documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if prisoners, Muslim prisoners, were made available and used by members of the Convicts Battalion for labour, to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that. All I know is that there were refugees, many refugees, in the students hostel in Siroki Brijeg but nobody forced them to work. I know nothing about others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Andabak called an order for prisoners to be turned over to the Convicts Battalion, as is indicated in this document, 601?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document can say anything it likes but I never saw any document and I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any Muslim prisoners being held at the tobacco station in Siroki Brijeg during the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw a single one. Had I seen them, I would have told you, but I did not. Therefore...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Meek:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness NK, you testified that in 1992, Mr. Naletilic was a commander or the commander, one of the commanders, of the Convicts Battalion, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time, did -- was it common or not common that soldiers referred to the Convicts Battalion as "Tuta's unit"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said that I was a member of the Tuta's unit, I always said that I was in the Convicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a member of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, I was a member of the Convicts Battalion but I didn't have to say that I was Tuta's. Nobody said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you have misunderstood my question. My question is not whether you or other members of the Convicts Battalion referred to the Convicts Battalion as Tuta's unit. My question was: Did other soldiers, other people in the public, people who were not members of the Convicts Battalion, did they refer to the Convicts Battalion as Tuta's unit? If you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, there were all sorts of stories. I mean, people who had never seen Tuta were talking about that, about that unit, but they had never been there and it only means...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified, sir, about an individual by the name of Predrag Mandric [phoen] - and I may have mispronounced that name - also known as Lija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that you would see Lija in Siroki Brijeg in 1993 from time to time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what kind of occasions that you would see Lija in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see him in coffee bars, sitting with people, with girls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness NK, do you have any personal knowledge as to where Lija actually resided, what town or city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Siroki Brijeg, in Lise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P601, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you do not -- you've never seen Ivan Andabak's signature so that you cannot testify whether he signed that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say because I never saw such documents nor did anybody show them to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the signature on that document, P601, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Andabak's signature looks like. I did not have to see it, I did never see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you read the signatures, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Andabak," what is handwritten could be "Andabak," but I'm not certain. I never saw it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seric? Thank you very much. Any questions from the Judges? Yes, Judge Clark. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness NK, could you help me with this: Could you describe in a little more detail the circumstances in which Mr. Naletilic retired from being commander of the KB.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know much about that. I only know that he had some health problems, and that's why he retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It appears to me, Witness NK, that yesterday when you were asked, you actually remembered when he retired and I just wondered why the date came to mind so readily.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was there. I live there. And I told you that it was approximately, either in July or August, 1992. I can't actually tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And that's all you can assist the Chamber with, just that you lived in Siroki Brijeg and it was approximately the summer of 1992? You know nothing else? Was there a ceremony? Was there a handing over? Did you become aware that your commander had changed? Nothing like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no ceremonies at all. I don't know of any. If I could assist you, I would do that very gladly. What I told you -- what I knew I told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: How did you become aware who your new commander was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned from Mario Hrkac, Cikota, the late Cikota.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What did you learn from him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness NK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions? Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to help us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You were very kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We wish you a very pleasant journey back home. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any documents to tender, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm happy to announce there are no documents to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do have documents to tender. Could I provide that list to the Trial Chamber at the end of the upcoming break? I cut out a lot of documents from the outline so I'm not sure what in fact I do want to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I also understand that some of the documents you used have been admitted already --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- so there is no need to submit those documents once again. Yes, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If I may assist, I believe 931A and 931B were the only two tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. President, we would offer 931A, 931B. I'll double check over the break but I have no reason to think that the registrar is wrong on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for those two documents, are there any objections? Because they are just a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: While they are bringing the witness, may I look at the documents for a moment, Your Honour? Those aren't translated. I understood yesterday those were going to be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We do have a translation that we can distribute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll admit those two documents after we receive the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: There will be no objection to those documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think for the record, those two which are the HVO identification card need to be under seal to protect the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Could we have the next witness, please. Are there any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for not replying promptly. I had to sort of rearrange my stuff here. We are asking for the same protective measures as for the previous witness, that's face distortion and a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Krsnik, your request for the protective measures is granted. Good morning -- yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise. Your Honour, before this witness takes the stand, I have for Madam Registrar, I apologise this morning, I need to give her -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Well, my break was rather short. I will continue the examination. I will try to be very specific and very efficient. Examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that this is the first time you find yourself in such a situation. We will give you some time to relax, to -- can you see the screen in front of you? Can you please follow the dot. When you see the dot stops -- as we speak the same language, we want to make the work of our interpreters easier. The most important thing is that my question and your answer do not overlap. Please wait before you start answering. Now you will be given a piece of paper on which you will find your name. Don't utter it, don't pronounce it, but if your name indeed is on the paper, just say yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever it says here is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please briefly tell the Chamber the date of birth, the place of birth, without saying your name. When were you born and where? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I was born on 31 May, 1964, in Risovac village, Jablanica municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber where you live now, today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I live in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber for how long have you lived in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I have lived in Siroki Brijeg since 1989.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live before that? In which town, or in another locality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Before that, I lived in my village, and in 1988 and part of 1989, I was in Western Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you some very specific questions and I'm asking for very specific answers from you. I shall focus mostly on 1993, and now I will first ask you a very general question: Were you in a military unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And if you turn to the substantive matters in your questions, we had better break here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, I put you a question but I'm going to repeat it. In 1992, and 1993, were you a member of any military unit in the HVO? And if the answer is yes, which unit was that? You don't have to wait that long.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I was a member of the Siroki Brijeg Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please assist this Chamber and tell them for how long were you a member of the Siroki Brijeg Brigade and can you please explain to the Chamber who the Siroki Brijeg Brigade was, which units were there in Siroki Brijeg, and can you please clarify the situation as far as you know it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: In late 1991, with the arrival of the Serbian reservists, Chetniks, in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, units organised themselves in neighbourhoods, in villages, in order to defend their homes, their villages, their towns. There were a number of such units in Siroki Brijeg. There was a headquarters in Siroki Brijeg. There was an infantry unit and a unit of engineers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. When you say that there were several battalions under the command of the headquarters, crisis headquarters of Siroki Brijeg, what kind of units were they? Were they volunteers, were they home guards, were they professionals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I already said that these were voluntary home guard units which were established by people themselves who gathered together, and I told them [as interpreted] what their goal was, to defend their homes. Those were home guards who defended at the distance of 10, 15 kilometres from their own homes. In Siroki Brijeg, there was also a unit called the Convicts Battalion which was active in all battlefronts in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of all these units in 1992? In Siroki Brijeg, that is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: In 1991 and in 1992, the commanding institution was the municipal headquarters. Up to April, 1992, the commander was Mr. Zlatan Tomas; and in April, Mr. Pero Cavar came and took the command of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody else organise -- participate in the organisation or just these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. There were other people who were then active in the municipalities. The municipal staffs were those who -- which were organised as any other units. There was Mr. Mikulic, Mr. Lasic, Mr. Culjak, Mr. Naletilic. I can't remember any other names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the role of Mr. Naletilic? What was his role, to your knowledge, in 1992? You mentioned his name as one of the people who were in the municipal Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naletilic was one of the men who were in charge of the defence of Siroki Brijeg, and as far as I know, Mr. Naletilic was one of the founders of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also head -- was he also heading the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, one can say that he was the head of the Convicts Battalion, together with Mr. Andabak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were there any changes in the organisation of these voluntary units during 1992 or 1993? Was it transformed into a bigger unit, a bigger establishment? How did that go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: During 1992, there were some minor changes: The units grew as the war went on, new people came, and these battalions existed up to the end of summer, 1992, and when the direct threat for Siroki Brijeg ceased and the war moved on to other areas, there was demobilisation, so the majority of people were put on reserve and only one battalion remained active. Another voluntary battalion that's -- battalion remained existing and manned the line facing the Chetniks. And there was also the Convicts Battalion that remained and it wasn't demobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a Siroki Brijeg Brigade? When was it established and when did it assume that name? If it existed, what kind of a unit was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I was also demobilised in either September or October, 1992, as the majority of other people, and I joined another unit when the brigade Mario Hrkac Cikota was formed on the 1st of July, and at that time, there was no money, there were no salaries. You have to understand that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any duty --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move to a private session? For, just for one question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, while you're on dates, I don't believe we've asked a year for the time that this witness joined the Cikota Brigade when it was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether it has entered in the transcript but the witness said it clearly, that after the demobilisation, he returned to the Siroki Brijeg Brigade which is now named after Mario Hrkac, Cikota, and that was in July, on the 1st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, the witness is too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the last question? Was it about the zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't ask you any leading questions. Can you please tell us in general terms what the Siroki Brijeg Brigade and the Convicts Battalion do in 1993? Did you have lines? Where did you go? Did you have a zone of responsibility? You have to tell us, I must not lead you into anything.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: In 1993, when I returned to the unit at the end of June or the beginning of July, I can't remember the date, we assumed a zone of responsibility in Djubrani, and the Siroki Brijeg Brigade was engaged there until I -- up until I left it. That was the 1st of April, 1994. And at the time, when I returned to the brigade, a part of the Convicts Battalion was with us. That was 25 men altogether. They were there all the time in the area of Djubrani as an intervention unit, and the men in the Convicts Battalion went through a lot. From 1992, they had a lot more experience, and our men found it much easier to be on the line when they knew that they had 20 men from the Convicts Battalion with them in case of an attack, in case of a line being --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness is too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you have to know that whatever you say in this courtroom has to be translated into the other two languages. You speak too fast so that the interpreters could not catch up with you. Make a pause after each sentence. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I'll try to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it did enter the transcript. You said Djubrani Vrdi. Where is Djubrani, just briefly, and where is Vrdi, and how long was your line that you manned? In either metres or kilometres, I don't know. So the first question is: Where is Djubrani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Djubrani is a village on a plateau and the general area is called Raska Gora, and Djubrani is one of the villages on that plateau. Vrdi is also on the same plateau and that plateau is north of Mostar. As far as the length of the line, the line that we manned, it was the canyon of the Neretva River, and for the most part it is rather inaccessible so there was no classic line in the proper sense of the word. We manned several checkpoints and as for the length of the area that was manned, I can't tell you precisely, but I believe that it was six, seven to eight kilometres. I can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you properly the Siroki Brijeg Brigade was there manning this line of six, seven kilometres and the Convicts Battalion's task was that in case of an attack on that line, then it would come from Djubrani to intervene on that same front line? Did I understand you, that that was what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you did. It was exactly like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, why is Djubrani important? Why is that an important feature and why were you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Djubrani, or rather that area, that front line which we manned, it was the defence of both Mostar and Siroki Brijeg. It is July, and at that time, there were frequent attacks of the Muslim units from the directions Sobrez [phoen] and Jablanica. So basically this is it. That was the defence of Siroki. Because I remember how in 1993, I remember it well, and Muslim units entered and took a feature on Cabolj, that is next to our brigade, and I remember well how at that time somebody said that about -- that they were at a distance of 8 kilometres from Siroki Brijeg as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Djubrani a part, conditionally speaking, of the Rastani theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Rastani is a village north of Mostar which is in a field below, in a valley, which is below Djubrani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but I mean Djubrani could be part of that front line, of that defence area of the Rastani theatre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You said a while ago, you mentioned Mr. Mladen Naletilic. Could you tell Their Honours how long have you known him, when did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I met Mr. Naletilic in the autumn of 1991. As for my relations with him, I could say that he was my father's friend mostly. We were but acquaintances. However, our families have been on friendly terms from before. That is, my late father and Mr. Naletilic's late father, they were friends and they were pretty close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you used to see Mr. Naletilic? And I'm talking about 1993 all the time. So in 1993, how often did you see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Well, we met now and then. I've already said that he was my father's friend and we met in Siroki Brijeg, around coffee bars, say, or when I went to see my father in the village, Mr. Naletilic was often there, for instance, on various holidays and on various occasions, and even I know that Mr. Naletilic's children came there on some holidays. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge if he held some office at that time, Mr. Naletilic, in 1993? Did he hold any office? Any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: As far as I know, in 1993, Mr. Naletilic did something in the municipal hall. I don't know what exactly but I know he did something in the municipal hall. And this is what I heard from my late father, and that is that Mr. Naletilic at that time had a company in Zagreb, precisely at that time in 1993, something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Naletilic had any military rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: You mean in 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: In 1993, nobody had any ranks, as far as I know. So to my knowledge, Mr. Naletilic did not have any rank and I do not know that any of us had any ranks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now the logical question: In 1992, do you have any knowledge if -- how many lads were in the Convicts -- and I call it Siroki Brijeg Convicts Battalion, how many lads were in that battalion? Because I believe that is its name; Siroki Brijeg Convicts Battalion, that is its full name, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, how many lads were in it, who commanded them, how many commanders were there? We heard here in the courtroom that there were officers -- an officer in the Convicts Battalion. That is what was said in this courtroom. In 1993, I mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: In 1993, the Convicts Battalion, and I make my assessment based on the number of men who were manning the front line in the area of Djubrani, and there could have been 20, 25 men, and there were three shifts, which means that they had some 60, 70 men. As for the commanders or officers, people with ranks, there were none. I mean nobody had any rank. There were people who were commanders and who came to those persons because we simply had 10, 15, 20 men and they would pick out the bravest, the best men from amongst them, and who in their eyes had some authority, and who could therefore lead them. In 1993, the Convicts Battalion, talking following the 1st of July, because the late Mario had already been killed. As far as I know, it was at that time led by Ivan Andabak and Zeljko Vukoja. It was the two of them, I don't know which sequence, who came after whom, but there were two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, you have to slow down. That's too fast for the interpreters. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as the Siroki Brijeg Brigade, did you conduct any operations or activities in April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: In April, 1993, I was not an active member of a unit and therefore I was not assigned anywhere but my unit, or rather a part of my unit, during the attack of the BH Army, part of my unit was engaged in the areas of Konjic and Jablanica, and that was at Easter time, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now my direct question to you: Did it take part, did it participate, in the action or whatever you care to call it, in the conflict in April, 1993, in a place called Risovac or Sovici or Doljani? Was it engaged there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. That is the conflict which I had in mind when I said it was engaged in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Honourable Court what you know about that? When was that? What happened? I will not ask you any questions, I will let you tell us all that you know about it. Just go slowly. Look at this dot.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: As far as I know, that conflict happened on Palm Sunday in April, 1993. I came to see my father. I came for two days. That is Easter falls on Sunday and the first day after Easter, after Sunday, that is Monday, that is another holy day. And in my village, we have the so-called Small Easter, which comes a week later. Now, and on proper Easter, we all gather, but it is only the family. And when the Small Easter comes, then other people also come and we go to attend the mass, and after the mass, after the mass, you invite guests to your house and there is a small feast. I remember how I came to see my father and that was right before the weekend. It was a Friday. It was a day before the attack. That is, on Friday evening, I came to my father's, and in the morning, my mother woke me up - I remember that well - that there were unusually many troops in the village. And I got up, got ready, dressed, and went downstairs, or rather, went out into the road and stopped a vehicle. And in this vehicle were the guys from my unit, from my -- the unit that I belonged to in 1992, and I asked them what was that about and why had they come? Because that was not the area which was covered by our unit. And one of them told me that they had received an order to go to the area of Sovici and Doljani because Mijat Tomic Battalion was blocked there. That was the unit which was active there, that they should go up there because that had been blocked, to link up with them, to see what it is about, and that there was nothing in particular. That is, I wanted to know because my father and my mother and my sisters and other of my relatives were there, so I naturally wanted to know what that was about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you? That the BH Army had undertaken any operation in those areas, Sovici, Doljani, Risovac, Jablanica? Or that they had been...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: There were some conflicts. There was some fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please -- I have to warn you. We have to slow down.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I believe that the previous day, there was some fighting between Doljani and Jablanica, and I do not know, a day or two before that, there was also some fighting in the area of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you heard that and what happened then? You talked to those troops and what happened then? What happened after that? Well, tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I went back home, and I told my mother that it was nothing, because at that time, there were frequently problems at the ABH checkpoint, somebody would be stopped there and you understand there were some individual things, and generally, the situation was very tense. And I told my mother that it was nothing to worry about, and I was calming her down, and as I was doing that, we could hear the detonations in the area of Sovicka Vrata. This is from my home to Sovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is that from your home, roughly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I understand that you are eager to give your testimony but you have to understand the main purpose for you to come here is to help us, the Judges, to understand what happened at certain periods in certain places. If you speak too fast, the interpreter could not follow you and some parts of your testimony might be lost in the transcript so that we could not be helped. So please make a pause after each sentence and control the pace of speaking. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must say that I'm -- the fault rests with me because I'm a professional but I also speed matters up. I start speaking faster. We speak the same language and then we start talking and then the interpreters cannot catch up with us. The last time that you heard -- you said was that you heard some detonations from the direction of Sovicka Vrata, and my last question was how far was that from your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: It is about two, two and a half kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when you talked with those soldiers and when you saw them, did you see Mr. Mladen Naletilic amongst them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No. Mr. Naletilic was with his children. He had come for Easter to see my father with his children. He was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were with him all the time that day, that day when it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: You mean when the attack happened? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting. Could we have the specific date when he says "that day"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Also, Mr. Krsnik, the last evidence that this witness gave was of a conversation when he was trying to calm down his mother, and suddenly Mr. Naletilic has turned up on the scene. I think you have to lay the ground a bit better than that. His mother woke him up, there were a lot of soldiers around, he went out and he spoke to the soldiers, he came back and he calmed his mother down. Now what happened after that? We heard nothing about Mr. Naletilic before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you heard Her Honour's question. Will you answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: The question was if my unit was up there, isn't it? Or is whether I recall the developments in April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear the question asked that -- that Her Honour asked you? I mean, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, you mentioned your mother, Mr. Naletilic in that. Will you shed some light on that situation. And my last question was whether you saw Mr. Naletilic among those soldiers and you said, "No he was at my father's." You heard Her Honour's question, so explain it; the date, when was it, how was it? All that is related to Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I said that our families -- that Mr. Naletilic was friends with my father and that he often came to see him when he had an opportunity to do that. And the same thing happened then, on that Easter day. Or for those Easter holidays. I said that I went to see my -- that I went to my father's on Easter and the first day of Easter. Mr. Naletilic came there, and that I'm talking about Monday, about Easter Monday, the first day after Easter. And we met at my father's. I was going to Siroki Brijeg because I was about to go to work. I returned to my father's on Friday evening, and Mr. Mladen Naletilic was still up there. And in the village, the situation was regular. That is, troops went through. I mean, naturally who communicated through that area. Men, you understand. And that morning, that morning, it was Saturday, I already said that my mother had woken me up and I went outside, that I halted a field vehicle and there were three or four guys from my unit, I recognised them in that vehicle. And I talked with them and asked them what it was all about. And they told me, as I have already said, that they had received an order and that the order was to go and link up with Mijat Tomic Battalion which had been blocked in Doljani, and which had -- was engaged in the fighting with the BH Army in the area between Doljani and Jablanica, and that some men from that unit had been prevented from getting towards -- from going towards Risovac and Jablanica, prevented by members of the BH Army, that the BH Army had set up its front line facing my village, in the areas of Borovnik and Pasije Stijene, and that it was not letting anyone through. But however, that there was still no open fighting, and that they had received no other order except to go there, link up with that unit, and be there to help it. And I returned home and I told my mother because I saw my mother again. I'm telling you of course she was afraid but I told my mother what I had heard from them and even in my other version, I told her that there was no problem at all, that everything was all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I think I saw Mr. Naletilic only after I entered the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it doesn't say -- you said that he had barely got up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, because he had spent the night in the house, that is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is not in the transcript. And were the children up already or were they still asleep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No, no, no, the children were not up yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, and what you heard, did you tell everybody in the house what you had heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, after I entered the house, because I saw my mother in front of the house. I told my father and Mr. Naletilic the whole story. I told you already that the version that I gave my mother was milder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did Mr. Naletilic react to that, if you can tell us, from your personal knowledge? What did do you in the house next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Well, he was worried because of the children, first of all. That was the reaction because that was the first time that fighting was happening that nearby, some fighting which was not expected or planned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you hear those detonations, sir, as you were talking with your mother or after you entered the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No. I was still in front of the house. Before I stepped into the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
