utterances.text: Tell me, please, now, this gun fire, the detonations stopped, or what happened that day? And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: After those detonations, one could hear small arms fire, and it went on all day long, from the hills above the village of Sovici. I have already mentioned that is the areas of Borovnik and Pasije Stijene. It was from that area the sounds reached us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course I'm not asking you to speculate and I may not do that, but do you know what caused those detonations? Do you know what weapons were involved? Because if I understand you well, you are an engineer, you are with the engineering units in the army. And who -- so what weapons were they fired from, the shells, and who was -- and who caused this fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Well, I was in the war in 1992, too, so I can say that these were detonations caused by mortars, not from some big guns, and it happened in the area behind Sovicka Vrata, that is, these shells were falling in the field and they were being fired from the direction of the positions of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Naletilic have a Motorola, or you, did you have any other communicating device? Did you see him therefore issue any orders to anyone, and any type of orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No. We did not have a telephone in the house, and as far as I know, Mr. Naletilic did not have a Motorola with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you with him all the time that Saturday and Sunday or I don't know how many days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: We were there that Saturday, Sunday. On Saturday evening, I remember somebody came, that is, troops were passing by all the time, and they would drop by. Some wanted, needed some water, some came to ask for some food, some came to have a coffee, but they kept passing through. And then suddenly somebody came and said that those on the positions up there had surrendered, that they were dead, that some had -- were pulled out. And that was Saturday evening. In the morning, there was no mass, there was no celebration of the holiday, so that on Sunday we were at home all the time. I remember that Mr. Naletilic wouldn't let his children come out and play outside, and the weather was -- the weather was very nice and yet he would not let them go out, and that he insisted that they remain in the house all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how old were they, were his children at that time? And do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Right now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we go into private session, please, for a moment, just in case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for a consultation with my client.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, when did Mr. Naletilic with his children leave? Where did he go and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Mr. Naletilic left my father's house, together with me, on Monday, on Monday evening. We left together. That Monday was a specific day because on Sunday, we received news that those guys down there had surrendered. The fighting went on but they are getting away from my village. On Monday afternoon, I remember two lads came. They were members of the Convicts Battalion. They came to our house and they told us that they had some killed men in Doljani and that, amongst others, Boro Barbaric was killed. Mr. Naletilic's reaction to that was a bit unusual, if one can call it that, because he said - I remember it very well - that Boka had been with him from 1991, and that he had to go and fetch his body, Boka's body, and he asked me to go with him. My mother, however, said, "Where do you want to go? He's dead. You can't help him. They will bring him, those guys who are up there." And the children also started crying. However, Mr. Naletilic went out of the house, got into the car with these two lads, asked me to watch his children. He got into the jeep with those two lads and went down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he return and what happened next? And what date was that, approximately, when he went there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: It was Monday, and on the following day, the late Mario was killed. So that was the -- on the 20th of April, and that date was 19th of April, because Boka was killed a day before Mario.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: They left, and I remained. He left with these two lads. He went to Doljani. I remained in the house. I was -- watched -- looking after the children. And they returned later in the afternoon, maybe two or two hours later. One of these lads returned and brought Mr. Naletilic back and Mr. Naletilic said to children to get ready. We packed their things, we packed our things, and we went to Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my final question: Yesterday, the -- Mr. Prosecutor gave us an exhibit. Can you please look at it and comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to give P931A to the witness. [In English] A and B. [Interpretation] I apologise. For the transcript, Mr. Meek warns me we are talking about Exhibit 931A and 931B, both by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What am I supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, on the right-hand side, there is the designation of the unit. What is "SBB"? What does that stand for, "S.B.B."?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: SBB on the ID, on the military ID.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: It could be the Siroki Brijeg Brigade but I cannot say that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That would be all from me, Your Honours. I hope I was specific. I was sufficient. I was watching the time, and I believe that I have used 45 minutes. 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the registrar calculated the time for you. Yes, Mr. Bos, for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and I believe that it took one hour and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I honour the way Madam Registrar keeps the time. But the examination went smoothly and it could not have been an hour and 20 minutes, and I am kindly asking for Madam Registrar's intervention, or we are really going to time ourselves because I'm planning to finish another witness, that's why I am trying to go very fast, and I am planning to have a number of witnesses tomorrow, whom I want to finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, according to my calculation, you used one hour for your direct examination and I guess Mr. Bos said he will take one hour and 20 minutes for his cross-examination. Am I right, Mr. Boss?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I thought it took one hour and 20 minutes. It may have been an hour. I may have been mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Bos:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just first for the record say this: That the summary of this witness, the Rule 65 summary of this witness is as follows: Witness will testify about 19th of April, 1993 when he saw Mladen Naletilic in the house of his father in Risovac. That's the summary and I think the Defence went a bit out of the scope of this summary, especially in the first part.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps Mr. Bos has not been supplied with the nearly two-page letter I sent to Mr. Scott on April 2nd outlining exactly what the testimony would be for this witness, but I certainly sent that letter after Your Honours requested that we do that and I believe it was the 2nd day of April, and it was nearly a page and a half to a page and three-quarters outlining the summary of this witness in great detail. So I can very easily get that letter for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In fact, I think I gave the Trial Chamber a copy of that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We did not receive that letter but, Mr. Bos, would you please clear it up for us, whether you have received this letter or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I haven't seen that letter, Your Honours, and if I would, I wouldn't read this summary out. I worked on the basis of the information I just read out. And Defence may be right but I have never seen that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Anyway, you may proceed until we have some problem with that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I have some exhibits for this cross-examination, and I will distribute that now. Cross-examined by Mr. Bos:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, good morning, my name is Roland Bos, for the Prosecution, and I will ask you some questions in cross-examination. Witness, you testified that you were a member of the Siroki Brijeg Brigade. Were you ever a member of the 3rd Mijat Tomic Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No, never, I was never a member of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe just to clear this up, could we have the witness be shown Exhibit P187.1, which is in that bundle. It's the first exhibit in this bundle. Mr. Usher, if you could show the witness Exhibit P187.1. Here, you can -- you can use this bundle. The first exhibit of that bundle, if that could be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this exhibit, maybe I can ask you, Witness, if you said that you were not a member of this Mijat Tomic Battalion, you did refer in your testimony to this battalion and you said that this battalion was involved in the combat activities around Sovici Doljani; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Please repeat the question, because I was looking at the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well let's look at the exhibit first, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe if we can put the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, I think this document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Everybody is furnished with this document so we can proceed without mentioning the identity of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you look at that document, could you please look at the name which is mentioned under number 1. Is it correct that that's your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No. It is not correct. The name is the same as mine but here it says --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't mention the name, don't mention the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could we go to private session, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, out of abundance of precaution, we will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I please ask when we will have a break, when is the time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think at 12.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, as I was saying, this man Rados was an HVO -- was a member of the 3rd Mijat Tomic Battalion and he made a diary of what happened. He was there at the time in Sovici-Doljani, he made a diary, and I would like to go through some of the parts which is written down in this diary. And maybe I should give you this version, as I will go through some parts which I have marked and it will be easier for you to read the marked parts which I will show to you. Now, the first part, which is marked, and this is a description of the day of 15 April, 1993, and I'll read out the part which is highlighted: "15 April, 1993, at 1230, the fighting started. Explosions and shooting from the directions of Risovac. Action approximately 1315. Ivan Rogic, Ivica Azinovic, followed by Ivica Tomic, Vlado Atunovic and Mato Krtic came down from Risovac. Up there everything was mobile, active and lively. They were ready to do the job in two days, to have coffee together in Jablanica. Many high-ranking officials, led by Miljenko Lasic, who is in command of the operations, were there along with the legendary Tuta Micika and his commandos, the Sirokobrijeski slavuji, artillery and mortar units and the like." Now, Witness, on the 15th of April, where were you on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: In Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And reading this, do you know a man -- there is a reference to a man named Micika. Do you know this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just reading this -- reading this -- this part, would you agree that -- that it looks like the HVO is preparing for an attack on Sovici-Doljani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: That's what it says here, but I don't know it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's move on to the second quote, which is, on your version, page number 14, and this is on the 17th of April, 1993. On the B/C/S version, it's page 14; and on the English version, page number 69. Now let's go back again on the 17th of April, where exactly you were from the morning to the afternoon. You've testified that you -- this is on the Saturday. You testified that you returned to your mother. Could you give me exactly the time that you returned to your mother on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: On the 17th of April? I returned 15 or 20 minutes later. I don't know what the time was but that was very early in the morning, around 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning. Maybe 8.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so you arrived at 8.00 in the morning on the 17th of April and you then stayed the whole day in the house in Risovac that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. I was at home all that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Tuta was there the whole day as well? You can testify here that you were with him the whole day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. He was there all that day, and his children were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the quotes on page 13 B/C/S version, page 69 of the English version. I'd like the Chamber -- to direct the Chamber's attention to the second paragraph on page 69, and it says as follows: "At 1105 hours we received an order that we must not touch any of the loyal civilians. This order was issued to Tuta too." And then I'll skip one paragraph, and then it says, "In an order, Protrka and Tuta agreed that anyone touching a civilian, woman or child shall be shot!!!" Witness would you not agree that from these two quotes I just read out to you, that Mr. Tuta was actually giving orders here on the 17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: This is what it says here, sir, but as far as I know, Tuta could not issue any orders. I was with him and if he had issued any orders, I would have known it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's move on, then, to B/C/S page number 16, and that's again the next highlighted part, page number 72 in the English version. On the 18th of April, about the second paragraph, it says -- this is on 18 April, Palm Sunday: "About 72 to 73 people surrendered in Sovici and returned their weapons. They put them up in a school. Women and children were taken to a separate location." Did you know that prisoners were -- that prisoners were taken on the 18th of April and put in a school in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that they were taken prisoners. Nobody said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move, then, on to 19th of April, this is the Monday. Now, let's first -- let me first ask you: On Monday, the 19th of April, what -- you left the house at what time and where did you go? You've said that you left with Tuta. Where did you go and at what time was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: We left the house in the evening. I think it was around 7.00 or half past 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You left together with Tuta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. I took him, because he was up there with his children and he did not have his car there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so that whole day, you and Tuta were again still in the house in Risovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. We were at home in the house in Risovac all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's read what is said here in this diary on the 19th of April. Direct the Trial Chamber's attention to page 74, starting with the third paragraph, and I'll read it out: "Tuta arrived almost exactly at noon. It is enough to see him once to remember him. He is of medium height, with greyish hair, and has a skinny face and sunken cheeks. He wears glasses with metal (golden) frames, his teeth are white and well preserved. His authority is great. He left an impression of a skilful warrior, someone somewhat like Odisej. Each of the fellows from his team were also characteristic, but you could see immediately that they are very good at warfare. I would not want to be their enemy. They all had nicknames, the names were not necessary. They immediately sat at the table with a map in front of them and started making a detailed plan. Tuta took everyone's comments into account, but the main decisions were his. The only other two who were consulted were Mico Lasic and Slavko Puljic; the others would only make suggestions." Now, Witness, this diary says that Tuta arrived on the 19th of April at noon, and this person who wrote the diary was in Doljani. Would that be possible, according to your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: What it says here is not possible because I already said that Mr. Tuta left my house on the 19th and he left late in the afternoon, around 4.00. That's when he left for Doljani. I don't know what he did there. He left around 4.00 in the afternoon, returned two or two and a half hours later, because already around 7 or half past 7.00 we left my house to go to Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you just testified before that you stayed with Tuta in the house up until 7.00 that evening and now you're saying that Tuta left at 4.00 without you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, he did leave without me, down there, and I said that earlier on. Because he went to fetch Boka's body. I said that on that day his friend who was in his unit in 1991 and 1992, was killed on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I understood that from your testimony that you left -- that you and Tuta left at 7.00 that evening and that Tuta did not leave the house before that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the 19th of April now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I'm also talking about the 19th of April, and I said earlier, and I repeat that, and this was to Defence counsel's question, that on the 19th, Tuta went to fetch his friend Boka's body, that two members of the Convicts Battalion who came to fetch him, that one of them returned him to my house, and that it was then that we got ready, packed our things and left for Siroki Brijeg. That was me, him, and his children.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think we can have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have major objections but I don't know whether my learned friend has finished his examination, and I will take your instructions. Did you finish examining the witness on this diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, not yet, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Usher, I have here the transcript as marked. I took it back just to highlight one other part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm just going to have a few more quotes from this diary. The next one is -- we left off with a quote on the bottom of that page, and then I just, a little more down, there is another piece of text which I want to read out to you which says the following: "Tuta was having" -- this is on page 75 of the English translation, Your Honour, second paragraph. "Tuta was having loza brandy, Mico and Slavko had the same, the others had nothing. Two men left a particularly strong impression. They were known as Cikota and Lija. They had short hair, were very strong and had a great clout. Then it started. A thunderous roar of fire from mortars, Bofors, two-barrelled guns and the like." Two questions arising from this quote. Witness, do you know the names Cikota and Lija which are mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I'm aware -- yes, I'm familiar with these names, or nicknames rather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were both in Sovici-Doljani around -- on that day? Did you see them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No. I did not see them, but I heard that they were there and Cikota was killed the next day, on the 20th, but I personally did not see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says also here that a thunderous roar of fire from Bofors. Did you see any Bofors in the area around that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No, I did not. I never left the house. I don't understand the question. I didn't go from my house to the place where the fighting was taking place. I did not see it. I already said that I was at home all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the last quote, which is on page 76 of the English version, and -- or the B/C/S version it's the last part of the 19 April description. And let me read it out to you. "A team came back soon after that. They asked Tuta to come outside. Those who knew the situation well said that something must be wrong. And something was wrong. Two of his men were killed during the mopping up operation. They were mowed down by a machine-gun. Tuta was angry and swearing; but he remained in control. 'We are at war, somebody has to die, but not on such a small assignment. Okay. We must go on.' And we did. There were no problems any more. Tuta said that he must go to Risovac to see his children whom he does not often get to see as they live in Germany. The majority of forces went to Risovac after him." Now, Witness, you were saying that on the 19th, Mr. Tuta left in the afternoon and came back in the evening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, it is. He left in the afternoon. I've already said that, around 4.00, late in the afternoon, and came back around half past 6.00 or somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew that somebody was shot. Did you hear that from him after he came back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No. When those guys from the Convicts Battalion came to Tuta to tell him that Boka had been killed and two other guys, and two other guys of the Convicts Battalion, and they came to tell Tuta that Boka had been killed. It was from them that I heard it. I was with him at the time when they told him that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know the names of these two guys who informed Tuta about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No, I don't. I did not know them personally. I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time did they arrive at the house to inform Tuta about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Well, they arrived, I don't know, around half past 3.00, all that was happening in the afternoon, not the exact time. What I know is that around 7 or half past 7.00, we went home. I know that Tuta did not stay more than two, two and a half hours because I stayed behind with the children. I had problems with them so that I was looking at the time very often, thinking whether he'd be back shortly. You know, because I could no more explain to the children where he'd gone or when he'd come back, and I expected him at any moment. So it could have been that they came half past 3.00, before 4.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, then, that when these two soldiers arrived and informed Tuta about the death of these other two soldiers, that after that, Mr. Tuta left the house and then came back around 7.00? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: My testimony is that before 4.00, two members of the Convicts Battalion came to my father's house where I was together with Tuta, and that they said that Boka had been killed. You understand? And Tuta then said that Boka was with him, in the same unit with him in 1991, 1992, and that he had to go to fetch his Boka. That is what he said. He asked me to come with him. And then my mother stood up and said, "Why do you have to go there? Neither of you has to go because they will collect him and you can't help him any way because he's already dead." And the children started to cry. Tuta stood up, went out, I followed, and he told me to look after the children, and he then sat in the car and left with these two guys and returned in two hours or maybe two and a half at the most. It was one of these Convicts Battalion guys who brought him back, and then we got the children ready, got in the car and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about when you left. So you said that in the evening of the 19th of April, you and Tuta left for Siroki Brijeg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Siroki Brijeg, that was the last time you saw Tuta? When was the next time you saw Tuta again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I saw him again at the funeral of the late Boka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what day was the funeral?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: The funeral was a day after Cikota's death. So it was the 21st.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you see Tuta again after that funeral?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I saw him the next day, at Cikota's funeral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after Cikota's funeral, when was the next time you saw Tuta again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot be precise. Perhaps a few days later or -- there was no any -- no particular occasion to remember it. I know, for instance, that then I saw him in Risovac again in August, when members who were killed when the ABH attacked Doljani were being buried, so between that 22nd of April and August, we might have met in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just let's go back a little. I just want to clarify a few other things. You've said that you were in Risovac on the 11th of April, a Monday, and that you then left and came back on the 16th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I was in Risovac on the 11th. It was Sunday. It was Easter. So Monday was the 12th. On Monday evening, I went to Siroki Brijeg because on that Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, I worked, and I came back then on Friday evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's Friday evening, the 16th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it correct to say that from the period of 11 April until Friday evening, the 16th of April, you didn't see Tuta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I did see Tuta on Monday, in the afternoon of the 12th of April when I went to Siroki Brijeg. He came before I left my father's house and so I saw him again on the 16th when I once again came to my father's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your testimony is that in that period that you were in Siroki Brijeg, Tuta was in Risovac, as far as you know? You didn't see him but...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, from what I know. I did not see him but from what I know, he did not go anywhere. He was there all the time with his children, because the children had come for Easter holidays and I suppose he seized that opportunity to be with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P299.1, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I expect your instruction was to raise the matter now because it has to do with this exhibit, and I'm referring to the one which we finished, and that is P928.2 because I have a number of very strong objections to that document. If you look at the document title, it says that it is a handwritten diary, but I do not see a handwritten diary anywhere, and what worries me even more is that when a protected witness was called here - and Your Honours will remember it was a witness from Jablanica, if you do - he was also shown this document, but it was not said that it was a diary and that is why I always say that one needs to be correct. You remember my objections. And finally it was admitted it was a diary. There were two pages which were written in -- handwritten. So first I should like to hear from the Prosecutor whether this is the document or the diary which they consider original or is there some other document which they deem is original, and if there is a document which is handwritten, could we finally get it? Or is this document considered the original? We want to hear it from them. And on the basis of what do they say that this is the diary of this gentleman when the source is the BH government? And I believe we've already established that there is no such thing as the Bosnian government. And what would the private diary do if it is? And that is why I doubt that it is, because it is only the Prosecution who claim it, but how could the Bosnian and Herzegovinian government come by this diary which, to cap it all, does not even exist? So that I presume it was the AID, as always. So we would like to hear which document is the original because it says here handwritten and this definitely is not handwritten. And could we finally get this integral document which they consider to be the original of the document? And the second thing, Your Honours, we once again call upon you to indicate -- to instruct that the examination be conducted correctly. It says here, Tuta, legendary man, and Micika, and the Prosecutor only said Micika, so he should have asked the correct question, whether he knows, whether he's familiar with the name legendary Micika, Tuta. Who is that man? And can we get, at long last, this document, the document which the Prosecution says is a diary, and if it exists in this handwritten form, then can we get it? Of course, if it exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: For the first point, I think we believe that Mr. Bos will enlighten us on the sources of this document. As for the second issue, Mr. Krsnik, I believe that the witness is furnished with this document, he read it in B/C/S version, and he knows that legendary Tuta and Micika was written there in the document. Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't know if it would be better if we first -- if I first finished the cross-examination of the witness before we discuss the diary and its possible admission. I would prefer to do it when the cross-examination of the witness is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed. And when we are at the stage of the admitting of the document, you may tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, do you have this exhibit in front of you? This is P299.1. I don't know if you read the document. It says this is an order from Commander Ivan Bago. Do you know that man, Mr. Ivan Bago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I know one Ivan Bago from the Posusje area and he was the commander of the engineers. I don't know if that is the same gentleman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This order says that: "Pursuant to an agreement with the commander of the southwest zone of the Herceg community, Brigadier Mico Lasic, with coordinator for Herceg-Bosna Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, with representatives of the Main Staff, Colonel Ivan Andabak, I issue hereby the following order PEE [phoen] Platoon and a reconnaissance squad are to be met -- are to be on 15 April, 1993, at ten hours, in the area of Sovicka Vrata." Now, witness, on the 15th of April, you were still in Siroki Brijeg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that it's possible Mr. Tuta was in this meeting at Sovicka Vrata on the 15th of April? Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I do not know that because I was not up there. And I'd rather not make any guesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how far is -- and I think you've testified but I just want to make sure again; how far is the house in Risovac where you stayed from Sovicka Vrata?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Two, two and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is Risovac from Doljani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Risovac from Doljani, some 12, 13 kilometres. Risovac-Jablanica, 27, Doljani somewhere halfway, so that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's just recapitulate everything and then this cross-examination will be over. I just want to confirm all the dates again. So you were in Risovac on the 11th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the morning of 12 April, you left for Siroki Brijeg and you came back in the late afternoon of 16 April, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I left late afternoon on the 12th of April, and I returned in the late afternoon of the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that on 17 and 18 April, you celebrated Easter in Risovac at the house together with Tuta, and you saw Tuta the whole day, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No. We were not celebrating anything because on the 17th the attack took place. Yes, the next day was to be a holiday but we did not celebrate anything. It was a holy day but there was no celebration because in the immediate vicinity, there was fighting. The church is halfway between my house and Sovicka Vrata but nobody could go to the church, nobody could attend mass because we couldn't go out. So we stayed at home, we were there, waiting for somebody to come and tell us what was going on. We would just come out in front of the house and try to listen to what was going on, the detonation and all that, whilst we could hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... soldiers be walking in and out of the house during those days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I've already said that, the soldiers did drop by. Some were hungry, somebody wanted water because he was thirsty, somebody wanted to have a cup of coffee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Tuta talk to these soldiers as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. We all talked with those soldiers. Tuta and I and my father, my mother, because we all wanted to know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the 19th of April, you're testifying that two soldiers came around 3.30 in the afternoon and informed Mr. Tuta that two soldiers from the Convicts Battalion had died in combat. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I said that they had come at about that time to tell Tuta that Boka had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Tuta left and he came back around 7.00 that evening, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. He left with them and returned before 7.00 because at 7.00, we were already on our way to Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the evening of the 19th, you left for Siroki Brijeg and then the next two occasions that you saw Mr. Tuta was on the 21st at the funeral of Boka and the 22nd at the funeral of Cikota, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Boka's funeral on the 21st and Cikota's funeral on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would have no idea what Tuta was doing from the evening of the 19th of April when you left for Siroki Brijeg and you departed in Siroki Brijeg. You would not know what Tuta did afterwards except that you saw him on the 21st at a funeral and on the 22nd at a funeral, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat the question, please? I wasn't with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you departed, after you went to Siroki Brijeg on the 19th of April, in the evening, you and Tuta departed in Siroki Brijeg, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, you would not know anything about the whereabouts of Tuta except that you saw him on the 21st at the funeral of Boka and on the 22nd at the funeral of Cikota, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. I cannot know because I wasn't with him at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if any houses were burnt in Doljani after the 19th of April, you would not know whether Tuta was involved or not because you were not at his side, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct. I have no way of knowing it. I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination? Mr. Krsnik? Re-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, just a few questions. I'm looking at the English transcript and now that I can follow it, and I think that they could be perhaps -- there might be some confusion. Of course it is not your fault, it is the transcript's fault, the transcript in the sense how I look at it. I hope nobody will misunderstand me this time and I apologise in advance, I merely want to clear this up. When was Easter, the date, the day, and the holiday, the week after Easter, what you call Little Easter, the day and the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Are you asking me? Easter was on the 11th of April, on Sunday, and the week later, the holiday was again on the 18th of April, Sunday again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And both are celebrated and observed equally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I said in my village, in my village, both those holidays are observed, but as a matter of fact, what we call the Small Easter was observed more because the -- because Easter itself is a family holiday, and the second one is the time when you invite all your relatives and friends to your house, you go to the church, you attend the mass, and then you come back and you have a luncheon. So that is in my village, in my house, it is specific and it is different from Easter proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you go to Siroki Brijeg on the 19th? With whom and by what means of transportation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: On the 19th, to Siroki Brijeg, I took my own car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was somebody with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I've already said it, Mr. Naletilic and his two sons were with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went together to Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, we went together to Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't be surprised. We lawyers do certain things in a certain way and we wish to establish certain things here. Yes, you said it already, you repeated it about a dozen times but when I look at the transcript, I hear questions posed to you by my learned friend and that's why I asked you that. I'm sorry, when you were asked by the Prosecutor how far is Risovac from Doljani, and you answered, did you mean by road or did you mean as the crow flies when you...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I meant by road, because I never took to air to go from Risovac to Doljani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, of course. Don't get cross with me. We have to ask this. Don't misunderstand our questions. And tell me how far is it as the crow flies, approximately, because of course you can't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: From Risovac to Doljani?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Well, I cannot affirm but I'd say it's six kilometres because it's a mountainous area, there are lots of curves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but was this road important? I mean Doljani-Sovici-Risovac, was that an important road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean exactly, but this road in 1992, yes, in 1992 it was called the Road of Salvation because it was used to pull out civilians from Central Bosnia, from the areas of Bosnia north of that particular area, pulling them out before the Serb aggression, it was called the Road of Salvation. And I and my units, amongst others, were also engaged in maintaining that road to keep it passable because it is a mountain road and it's not really a proper road. It's not for buses and large trucks so we in civilian companies and the military, we were all on that road, trying to maintain it. We simply tried to maintain it, to keep it in working order, especially wintertime. In wintertime, we had to clean the snow to make it passable so people could communicate normally. That was the only road that people could take to go to Bosnia and get food from there and come back. And that is why it was called the Road of Salvation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. My client is trying to tell me something but I think that I do not have any further questions. Tell me, do you personally know whether Mr. Naletilic personally participated in 1992 and made this road passable, liberated it during the battle for Mountain Cvrsnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes, it was either in April or in May, on the Mountain Cvrsnica, on its highest peak from which you could see the plateau and that road and my village, there was a former JNA feature which was controlled by the Serbian reservists, Chetniks, and Mr. Naletilic and the lads from the Convicts Battalion, I think it was either in April or in May, I can't say that for a fact, he organised an action, an operation, and they chased the Chetniks away from that elevation. If they had remained there, they could see that road at a length of 30 kilometres and it would have been an ideal spot for them to control the area, to control, to see the convoys of refugees and everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question: You were born in Risovac. Were you ever in Pasije Stijene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No, I was never personally in Pasije Stijene although it may seem so close it may surprise you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you whether you could see the complete Risovac from Pasije Stijene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No, you can't see a complete Risovac from Pasije Stijene. You can see a lot of it. You can see my house. You can see a narrow strip of the village and the fields below the hill. That is what you cannot see, the remainder of the village you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the judges? Judge Clark. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, I have a few questions that I need you to clarify for me, sir. First of all, are the villages of Rastani and Djubrani on the opposite sides of the Neretva River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have already said that they are on the same side of the river, and Djubrani is on a plateau and Rastani is lying low in the valley. At the same level with Mostar city. And Rastani is on a plateau in Raska Gora and Djubrani is one of the villages on that plateau of Raska Gora.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is Rastani part of the general municipality of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I know, yes, it is a municipality within the general municipality of Mostar. It is a village next to the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And what about Djubrani? Is that included in the municipality of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I know, yes, it is also included in the municipality of Mostar. I can't say that for a fact because I was -- I don't know what the political organisation was, the regional organisation, but I believe if Jablanica belonged to Mostar, then Djubrani also had to belong to Mostar because there was nothing in between but that village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If you know this, you can answer, otherwise obviously some other witness will deal with it but what is the distance if one travelled by car, between Rastani and Djubrani? Not as the crow flies but along the road.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I couldn't tell you for a fact. I can give you just my rough estimate, if you will allow me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That would be good enough.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Djubrani village and Rastani village, some six kilometres along the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to move to another part of the world and when you talk about "my house and my village," is that the same house and the same village as your father's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. That is my father's house. At that time, I did not have any other house. That's why I said that that was my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was that your parents' permanent house in this village which I don't want to mention because we are in open session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Yes. They resided there permanently. In 1993, after the attack of the BH Army in July, during that autumn, the village was empty because it had been ordered for all the civilians to leave the village, because the positions held by the BH Army and the way they waged war by infiltrating their groups of -- in-depth was a possibility for a group to come in and slaughter people in the village, that's why an order had been given for the civilians to leave the village so that in the period between August or September, 1993, until the -- until the spring or January or February 1994, the village was empty, and my parents spent that period of time in Siroki Brijeg. They were not in their own house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to clarify that the house in the village was your parents' permanent house and where you had grown up and for a period, they had to leave it. Is that correct? Because of the wartime situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can you describe to me how -- what the facilities of the house are? Is it a house that has land around it or is it actually in a village with houses beside it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: My village is very specific so to say. It is composed of several hamlets, three or four or five houses stand together. Where my house is, there is my house and there are some other facilities like barns, the old barn, the new barn, there is my father's uncle's house, who he died and my father inherited his uncle's house. And we also used it as our residence. We resided in it. And there is also a house belonging to one of my relatives, with out houses as well; barns, garages, and one house is about 20, 30 or 50 metres away from another. They are very close to each other is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What I wanted to know, because I was curious what you would do the whole week with all family members and children all in one house, so the situation is that you had several houses in a unit of one residence. Was Mr. Naletilic and his children, were they residing in the main house, so to speak, with your parents, or in one of the guest houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Mr. Naletilic and his children stayed in my father's house. They slept there, they stayed there. And as for the part of your question what could one do with children for a week, I can tell you that my village is at a level of 1200 metres above the sea level. It is a mountain plateau between two mountains whose names are Vrana and Cvrsnica and the slopes of both these mountains are forested, Cvrsnica a bit more than Vrana. At one end of that plateau, there is a lake called Blidinsko Lake, and the complete area is beautiful to look at, and in 1995 or 1996, one part of that area was proclaimed a park of nature. In that area, in its lower part, there is a lot of pine trees, and when it is flourishing in the spring, it's -- there is a lot of dust, and very many families at the time who have problems with breathing, they come to this area, to this very day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I didn't expect so much detail but thank you. What I wanted to ask you is when you came to visit at your parents' house for the traditional Easter and then you had to return to work, did you bring your wife and children with you and did they remain in the house when you went back to Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: At that time, I did not have a wife and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I understood you to say that you had children who were the same age as Mr. Naletilic's children. I understood that they played together.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: No. My sons now are of the same age as Mr. Naletilic's sons were at the time. That's how I could remember how old were Mr. Naletilic's children at the time. That's how old my sons are now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You can understand now when I was asking what did you do with four children if they couldn't go outside. What I want to know is that you left to go to work, now that explains, and you left Mr. Naletilic with his two children and your mother and your father and possibly you said a sister. When you came back on the Friday, you said there were a lot of soldiers around or more than usual, and the following day, you heard noises that alarmed you, and you did your best to settle your mother down and not to worry her and then you told the truth and the reality of the situation to your father and Mr. Naletilic. What I'm curious about was why didn't you, Mr. Naletilic and the children leave to go to somewhere safer immediately you heard the shooting? Why didn't you take them in your car to Siroki Brijeg? Why did you stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, the large concentration of the troops did not happen on the 16th but on the morning of the 17th, and when my mother woke me up, she did it for precisely that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Why didn't you leave? Because Mr. Naletilic was obviously worried for his children and your mother was obviously upset.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Mr. Naletilic was concerned for his children's safety but I already told you that the -- what was the -- what was the practice of the BH Army, that they would infiltrate their sabotage groups in depth of the territory where it was least expected so the road was simply not safe enough, and as the conflict progressed, it went further away from our house, so that even on the following day, I can say that it was not necessary for any of to us leave the village, because on the evening of the 17th, we learned that in the positions that were closest to the village, to my village, that in these positions that the BH Army members had surrendered and that the fighting was moved from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: One last question: You know the area very well. At the time in 1993, did you know anything about there being a trout farm or a fish farm in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: I don't know. There is no such thing in my village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In the area. Do you know anything at all about a place where fish used to be raised, commercially or whatever, but not naturally any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know. I know that on the Neretva River there was a floating something, I can't give you the technical term but it was the area where fish was grown or raised. On the Neretva River. As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do not worry if you do not know the answer but thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions? Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question Further examination by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the village had to be evacuated. What exactly had happened and why did you have to evacuate? That is what Judge Clark also asked you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NL
utterances.text: On the 27th of July, there was an attack by the BH Army on villages Sovici, Doljani and Risovac. Then the civilians were slaughtered because the attack followed their routine, their sabotage groups were infiltrated in the back and nobody expected it, and in Stipica Livada, there was a slaughter which took place. I believe that you all heard about that. That's when 27 civilians and HVO soldiers were killed, from an ambush, and there were also some killed civilians in Doljani. I don't know their exact number. After that, on the 29th and the 30th of July, a -- they were pushed back from this location, from Stipica Livada, and the villages of Sovici and Doljani were liberated, but drawing a lesson from that experience in order to prevent that from happening again, civilians were evacuated from Sovici, Doljani and Risovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, thank you, Witness, for coming to The Hague to give your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just remain where you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bos, are you ready to tell us about the source of that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Let me just first explain a little bit the background of this diary. First of all the diary consists of three different documents. You have the handwritten diary, you have the typed out diary both in the B/C/S language and then you have the English translation. The typed out B/C/S version of this diary was disclosed to the Defence this September 2000. At that time we did not have the handwritten diary. We just had the typed out version in B/C/S. The handwritten version we received later, and the handwritten version, together with the English version and the complete diary, was then tendered by Mr. Poriouvaev through Witness NE, if I remember well, on the 29th of May. I can also inform the Trial Chamber that we don't have the original original version of the diary. We only have a copy of the handwritten diary. So that's the background, and that explains why we did not disclose the handwritten diary in September, 2000. Now, on the 29th of May, when the diary was tendered through Witness NE by Mr. Poriouvaev, the Defence made an objection to the admission of this diary and that objection is still pending before the Trial Chamber. And just on the admission of this diary, I'd like to say that obviously the best person to authenticate this document is the author of the diary, Mr. Rados, but we are not in a position to call Mr. Rados, and we submit that this document can also be admitted without Mr. Rados. The Appeals Chamber has said that on evidence that there is no legal basis, the proof of authenticity is a separate threshold requirement for the admission of documentary evidence and I think you've been referring -- your Chamber has been referring to this Appeals Chamber decision as well. And it's our submission Your Honour that is if you read the contents of this diary, and you put that in the context of the evidence that the Prosecutor has presented on Sovici-Doljani, the document authenticates itself. If you read it would be very unlikely that this whole document is a forgery. And that's why I think this document should be admitted. That's what I need to say on the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could I just ask a question about that, Mr. Bos? Originally when it was furnished to you by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you received the typed up version, I think you said, and that was disclosed to the Defence. I believe you said that you subsequently received a photocopy of the handwritten version. Do you have the entire diary in photocopy form, including the first and last page and the continuation pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, that is Exhibit P928. That's the entire diary and that was tendered by Mr. Poriouvaev through Witness NE. And what I have used today is Exhibit P928/2, which are excerpts from this diary, and I think that the Trial Chamber should have a complete copy of that diary. I think that was submitted on the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how -- where the diary was found, who typed it out, when it was typed out, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't give you information. We can investigate this but, at the moment, I don't have any information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is there any person who might subsequently be in a position to improve the pedigree, if you like, of the provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We can try, Your Honours, but at the moment I can't say anything more than I just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think what I'm saying is music to the ears of Mr. Naletilic's counsel but obviously a diary containing extracts that are very pertinent has to be looked at with care.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I understand your comments, Your Honour, and we can try to do this and maybe in the rebuttal case we could call a witness who could say more about this diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this Trial Chamber is considering the admission of this document at this moment. Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, I know Mr. Krsnik wants to address. I just want to address one issue. If this diary is admitted into evidence, we might as well, the Prosecution might as well quit calling live witnesses. They might as well just get statements and put them into evidence, because at that point, our client's right to a fair trial, the right to confront his accusers and the witnesses against him are gone, absolutely gone. That's the bottom line, as far as I'm concerned, for the procedural issue, and the fundamental right to a fair trial. Mr. Krsnik has other observations, but that's my observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll take your objections into consideration. Yes, Mr. Krsnik? Are you not talking about the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Well, I will be talking about the same thing but something which is much more important because somebody keeps warning me, interrupting me and I simply can't focus on the things that need. We never received the alleged handwritten diary. I think the Defence should have been given that because what Mr. Poriouvaev tendered was two pages, and we got two pages of the handwritten diary. So let us first establish the accuracy of what we are saying. Never the whole diary, handwritten, as it is said. The whole handwritten diary has never been tendered and we never received. Only two pages of it. That is one thing. Secondly, it is precisely with this diary in mind that the Defence will endeavour to prove all the AID forgeries, because this is typewritten in Ekavica dialect, and a man who is a Croat or a man of Croat origin, he would never use that particular dialect in which this is typed out. Thirdly, perhaps I did not say this, but now we have no time for any ex parte sessions, when I say Ekavica dialect, I mean the Serbian dialect. I'm saying that this was not in Croatian language. And the third thing, Your Honours -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course, the Defence is trying to at least get the names of these people, this Alojz Rados and others, and so far we have not heard any, or at least the Defence has not found it but we shall continue dealing with this because this is the -- in the Defence's interests because it is this document that I'd like to use to show what is being done with the documents that reach this Tribunal through the Bosnia-Herzegovina government so we shall continue our investigation to try to find, to locate this Mr. Alojz Rados, and I might say I have serious doubts about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the Prosecution has the obligation to furnish the handwritten documents to the Defence counsel. That could be fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I may be misunderstanding but it's my understanding that on the 29th of May, when Mr. Poriouvaev cross-examined Witness NE, this is the complete diary. This binder was given to the Defence and also to the Trial Chamber. And it's true that Mr. Poriouvaev only used two excerpts from this diary but this complete binder was, at that time, given to the Defence. At least, that's how I have understood it. That if that's not the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have no idea about that but anyway, you have the obligation to furnish the whole diary to the Chamber and to the Defence counsel if you want to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Of course if it's not done, we will definitely do, but it was my understanding that it was already done and if it's not the case, then I apologise because that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I was just thinking that if -- give me the exact number, I will check my records, and if I have it, I'm sure everyone has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Exhibit P928.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At the same time, I would like to invite Defence counsel to submit written objections to the admission of this document into evidence, listing all the arguments you expressed here concerning this document. Well, could we have the next witness? Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, sorry, Your Honour. Just a couple of things because I'm afraid if we wait until the end, as usual, sometimes it's hard to get things done right at the end of the sessions. Two things: In terms of the documents tendered through Mr. Stringer's witness, prior witness, the Chamber had asked about that, and just to facilitate, try to make this a bit easier, I think there is only -- my understanding from Mr. Stringer correctly, there is only one other of the exhibits that we would tender, which is P663.1. So it's a very short -- it was a very short document about the six prisoners that were sent to work on Zeljko Bosnjak ATG, I think out of the bundle that was originally prepared, that's the only one in addition that Mr. Stringer -- that we would tender, 663.1. That is one item, Mr. President. Mr. President, the second item is very important to us. In the last -- since starting at least yesterday, and again today, counsel for Mr. Naletilic has made several references to the fact that there is something -- I've heard, frankly, a number of different numbers, but somewhere between the vicinity of 12 to 15 witnesses already in The Hague. Now, if that's true, I'm not going to mention any -- perhaps we could go to private session for just a moment to be safe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we are in the open session. Mr. Meek, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The one other matter I would like to bring up. I don't want to beat a dead dog, so to speak, but we filed a motion for a reasonable break before the depositions. The Prosecutor this morning said he doesn't intend to file a written response. They filed a motion several weeks ago to change the hours from the afternoon to the mornings, or on some schedule. Your Honours ruled on that the very next day, not giving the Defence the proper seven day notice to even file a written response to. As Mr. Seric points out, we have arrangements to make, plane reservations, a lot of things to do. We very much would like to know as soon as humanly possible what will happen. And I would also say that we've had this argument from the Prosecution on our motions where we allege some prejudice and they always come back with, well, all they say is prejudice. I hear Mr. Scott's argument this morning and all he says is I do not object as long as we are not prejudiced, but he hasn't told you, he hasn't told us how he's prejudiced, it's just an allegation. I honestly don't believe they have an objection to this break, but I think we all need to know. That's all I'm asking Your Honours, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. Scott, please be very concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, and Mr. Stringer will respond further on his exhibit and then I apologise if I spoke for him. Your Honour, I thought I was clear this morning. I will be brief. The prejudice is this: In theory, we would not object to a break, if it's reasonable and assists the Chamber and assists the counsel and everybody. The concern was this, that it becomes, frankly, the tail wagging the dog, that a schedule is then set and it becomes artificial and it dictates certain things. And the concern was that because of a schedule and because then a break and everything else being set and a break before and a break after, that the pressure would increase to finish these witnesses in a way that would then impinge on the effective cross-examination of the witnesses, that there would be timetables that would not allow us to conduct effective cross-examination. That's the potential prejudice and that's what we objected to. If the Chamber -- I want to choose my words -- I'm not asking for guarantees from the Chamber, I'm not sure that's the right word. As long as the Chamber recognises our concern and that if we don't finish by -- if there is a break on some date and if the witnesses are not effectively finished by then and we have not had the chance to conduct effective cross-examination and we call all those witnesses in the future and we have the opportunity to conduct an effective cross-examination, then we don't object -- then in that circumstance, I don't think we would object to breaks. We do object if it's going to become - if I can use the phrase again - if it becomes the tail wagging the dog, then we do object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, no more debates. Mr. Stringer, I give you one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. Counsel asserted that the document is neither relevant nor probative. I respectfully disagree. I believe -- I don't have the -- I can't get to the transcript from my position here but I think in fact counsel authenticated this document, or at the very least referred to it in his redirect examination of the witness in which he called upon the witness to read the name of the person who signed the document, Ivan Andabak, which the witness did. Now, we have got a document here that bears the stamp, the original language version bearing the stamp from the Zagreb archive. We've reported and informed the Trial Chamber in our list that it is in fact a document from the Zagreb archive. It is a document bearing what appears to be the signature of Ivan Andabak over the typed name of Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, as the commander of the Convicts Battalion, requesting the use of six prisoners from the Ljubuski prison for the use of the Convicts Battalion. We assert that it's authentic. It's probative, relevant, and ought to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This Trial Chamber would like to make the decisions in the admission of those documents at a later stage, taking into consideration of the views expressed by both parties. As for the decisions for the break, this Trial Chamber will make a decision this week no matter we received or not any written submissions from the Prosecution. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the same courtroom.
